summary: Describes how deployed MPLS networks do Equal Cost Multipath and gives best practices for applications that want to avoid the packet reordering that comes from sending a flow's packets over different paths. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: MPLS routers may split traffic over equal-cost paths after guessing that a payload is IP. RFC 4928 tells payload designers which starting values to avoid so one flow is less likely to arrive out of order.

subtitle: Rules for MPLS payload designers to reduce packet reordering caused by equal-cost paths.

tldr.problem: Some MPLS routers guess that a payload is IP by reading its first nibble. A non-IP payload that looks like IPv4 or IPv6 may be spread over equal-cost paths, reordering packets in one flow.
tldr.mechanism: Payload formats must forbid first-nibble values 0x4 and 0x6. Applications that require in-order delivery must restrict the first nibble to 0x0 or 0x1.
tldr.outcome: The recommendations offer a cautious way to avoid unwanted ECMP treatment, while acknowledging that the first-nibble test is a heuristic. RFC 4928 is BCP 128 and has been updated by RFC 7274 and RFC 9790.

today: RFC 4928 is a Best Current Practice published in June 2007. It has been updated by RFC 7274 and RFC 9790, and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Equal-Cost Paths Can Reorder Packets
sections.content:
Equal Cost Multipath (ECMP) lets a router share traffic across routes with equal cost. This can reduce delay and congestion, but packets from one flow may use different paths and arrive out of order. Application designers cannot control the forwarding choices in every MPLS network.

RFC 4928 describes deployed MPLS ECMP behavior and recommends payload rules for applications that need to avoid packet reordering.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can send packets from one flow along different routes with equal cost. If those routes have different delays, the packets may arrive in a different order.

sections.title: How Routers Guess What the Payload Is
sections.content:
An MPLS label stack does not identify the payload protocol directly. The bottom label's Forwarding Equivalence Class identifies it, but a router may not know that label binding. Some equipment therefore inspects the first nibble after the label stack and treats values 0x4 and 0x6 as IPv4 and IPv6.

If a non-IP payload begins with either value, the router may hash fields at that position as if they were IP addresses. It can then distribute packets of one flow across multiple paths. Changing labels between packets can also affect label-based load sharing.
sections.plainLanguage: Some routers inspect the first four bits after the MPLS labels to guess whether the payload is IP. A non-IP format can accidentally trigger that guess.

sections.title: When the Guess Has No Harmful Effect
sections.content:
The RFC describes cases where being mistaken for IPv4 may not split a flow. In an IPv4 VPN, the payload really is IP, so equipment can often find the IP header and make its normal ECMP choice. In another case, the values used by the router's hash remain constant across the flow, so the same path is selected.

These cases depend on how a network happens to process the payload. The recommendations do not rely on them.
sections.plainLanguage: A router's guess may be harmless when the payload really is IP or the values it hashes stay constant. These are special cases, not a design guarantee.

sections.title: Payload Values to Avoid
sections.content:
An Application Label is the label at the bottom of an MPLS stack that identifies an application's payload format. To avoid being mistaken for IP, that format must not allow 0x4 or 0x6 in the payload's first nibble.

Applications that depend on in-order delivery are required to restrict the first nibble to 0x0 or 0x1. This also avoids future equipment that might inspect values assigned to later IP versions. If an IP version using 0x0 or 0x1 is defined, equipment following this practice could not inspect that IP header for ECMP hashing.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not let a non-IP payload start with 0x4 or 0x6. If the application needs packets in order, use only 0x0 or 0x1 for its first nibble.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the worst result from misuse of these mechanisms would be packet misordering and possible throughput loss. An attacker would need to change a router's configuration or implementation, or alter packet bits on the wire, to cause that result.

IANA marked 0x1 as Reserved in the IP version-number space and added a reference to RFC 4928 for 0x0 and 0x1. The document does not change the allocation policy for version numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: The main risk described is packets arriving out of order, which can reduce throughput. The RFC also records the relevant version-number values with IANA.
